records.title: Cardiovascular responses with standard and extended bladder coverage G-suits during rapid decompression
records.locator: Subjects p. 209; Procedures and Results p. 210 (PDF p. 2)
records.note: Eight participants were tested in both garment conditions on separate days at least 48 h apart. The authors report no DCS symptoms and no Doppler VGE during the two test series. Practice runs are outside the measured comparison.

observations.protocol: Combat Edge condition. Randomized crossover, seated under positive-pressure oxygen. At least 60 min breathing 100% oxygen at ground level. After a 22,500-ft control, a brief excursion to 35,000 ft and return to 22,500 ft preceded rapid decompression to 60,000 ft in less than 0.6 s. Planned peak dwell up to 3 min. The same eight people underwent both conditions.
observations.outcome_window: During the published study observation. Fixed clinical follow-up was not specified.
observations.locator: Subjects p. 209; Procedures and Results p. 210 (PDF p. 2)
observations.note: The zero applies to the published test series. Exact clinical surveillance duration and delayed follow-up are unspecified.

records.title: The effect of increased G-suit coverage on the cardiovascular effects of positive pressure breathing at 60,000 ft
records.note: Preliminary report with six participants and the same two garments and 60,000-ft profile. Participant linkage to the later eight-person article is unavailable. The abstract supplies no DCS or VGE count.

records.title: Rapid decompressions up to 60,000 feet wearing the standard oxygen mask
records.note: The Brooks report describes seven rapid decompressions above 50,000 ft in five people. It reports acute oxygenation and hypoxia effects. Systematic DCS ascertainment and any DCS numerator are unavailable for this scope.

records.title: Lung volumes, pulmonary ventilation, and hypoxia following rapid decompression to 60,000 ft (18,288 m)
records.note: Six people made 12 rapid decompressions with two regulator conditions. One person developed severe hypoxia. The authors discuss spacing runs to limit DCS risk. A systematic DCS outcome tally and VGE assessments are unavailable.

records.title: Human physiological responses to positive pressure breathing for high altitude protection
records.locator: King’s College London staff profile, Education; Lee and Hay discussion and bibliography
records.note: Thesis identity verified. Lee and Hay describe 135 rapid decompressions with no reported DCI in their secondary discussion. The thesis, risk sets and surveillance window remain unverified. The secondary zero was kept out of the outcome tables.
